title: Your own or someone else's
goal: Master *sin/sitt/sina* — a word modern English no longer has, which separates "his own mother" from "someone else's mother" without a single extra word.
bekal: when to use *sin/sitt/sina* and when to use *hans/hennes/deras*
one test that always works: who is the subject of the sentence?
the verbs *ringa* and *hälsa på*, and the business of calling family

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Söndagssamtalet
dialogs.intro: Sunday afternoon. Oskar has just hung up the phone. Dian, who has just done the same with her family in Bandung, is curious about Swedish family habits.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Jag ringde min mamma. Jag ringer henne varje söndag.
lines.id: I called my mom. I call her every Sunday.
lines.literal: I called my mom. I call her every Sunday.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ringer Elin också sin mamma på söndagar?
lines.id: Does Elin call her mom on Sundays too?
lines.literal: calls Elin also her-own mom on Sundays?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Nej, hon ringer sin pappa. Hennes mamma bor i Norge.
lines.id: No, she calls her dad. Her mom lives in Norway.
lines.literal: no, she calls her-own dad. her mom lives in Norway.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vänta — sin pappa och hennes mamma? Varför inte samma ord?
lines.id: Wait — sin pappa and hennes mamma? Why not the same word?
lines.literal: wait — her-own dad and her mom? why not same word?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: För att Elin är den som ringer. Då säger vi sin.
lines.id: Because Elin is the one doing the calling. So we say sin.
lines.literal: for that Elin is the-one who calls. then say we sin.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Och i andra meningen är mamman ämnet, inte Elin.
lines.id: And in the second sentence, the mom is the subject, not Elin.
lines.literal: and in second sentence-the is mom-the subject-the, not Elin.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ett till: Ahmad tog sin cykel eller hans cykel?
lines.id: One more: Ahmad took sin cykel or hans cykel?
lines.literal: one more: Ahmad took his-own bike or his bike?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Sin, om det är hans egen. Hans, om det är någon annans.
lines.id: Sin, if it's his own. Hans, if it's someone else's.
lines.literal: sin, if it is his own. hans, if it is someone else's.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Då tog han hans cykel. Min cykel står ju kvar!
lines.id: Then he took someone else's bike. Mine's still here, after all!
lines.literal: then took he his bike. my bike stands after-all still!

notes: **The test that always works:** ask *who is the subject of this sentence?* If the owner of the thing **is the subject**, use *sin/sitt/sina*. If the owner is **someone else**, use *hans/hennes/deras*. There are no exceptions at A1 level.

**Han ringer sin mamma** = he calls his (own) mother. **Han ringer hans mamma** = he calls his (some other man's) mother. The two sentences mean different things and both are grammatically correct, so nobody will correct you — people will simply understand something you didn't mean.

**Sin is never the subject.** You will never see a sentence that starts with *sin*. It always sits in a part of the sentence that is **not** the subject: the object, an adverbial, or after a preposition. If you are tempted to write *Sin mamma ringer…*, that's a sign the sentence should be *Hans mamma ringer…*

**Ringde** is the past tense of *ringa* — group 2a, so the ending is *-de*. The past tense is covered fully in Unit 15; for now, just recognize that *-de* and *-te* at the end of a verb mean past time — much like English *-ed*.

**Fatta** means "get it, catch on" in everyday speech — more casual than *förstå*. *Jag fattar inte* (I don't get it) is heard constantly among young people, while *jag förstår inte* (I don't understand) is more neutral and safe in any situation.

**Ju** in *Min cykel står ju kvar* is a flavoring word meaning roughly "after all" or "you know" — it reminds the listener of something they already know. Together with *nog* (probably) and *väl* (surely?), these three words often go untranslated but change the whole feel of a sentence.

grammars.title: Sin, sitt, sina
body: The form follows the thing owned, exactly like *min/mitt/mina*. What decides whether to use it at all is the subject of the sentence.
after: **Sin is only for the third person.** With *jag*, *du*, *vi*, *ni* the question never comes up: in *jag ringer min mamma* it is already clear whose mother it is. So the whole *sin* business only concerns *han*, *hon*, *den*, *det* and *de*.
When the subject is plural, the form is still *sin/sitt/sina* — not *deras*: *De städar **sina** rum* (they clean their own rooms) vs *De städar **deras** rum* (they clean other people's rooms).

Norwegian and Danish have exactly the same word, and so did Latin (*suus*). English lost it, which is why *he called his mother* is genuinely ambiguous in English — his own mother, or another man's? That ambiguity never happens in Swedish.

grammars.title: Four sentences that show the difference

head: Sentence
Subject
Meaning
rows: Her brother is a student. (*sin* is impossible here)
Both of them are part of the subject, so not *sin*.

after: The fourth row is the trap that catches even intermediate learners: once the owner **is part of the subject itself** (*Anna och hennes bror*), *sin* can no longer be used. The reason makes sense when you think about it: *sin* always points **back** to the subject, and something can't point back to itself inside the same subject.
For A1, the first three rows are enough. The fourth row is here so you recognize it when you meet it later — not for memorizing now.

blocks.text: **Hälsa på** and **hälsa** are a treacherous pair. With the particle *på*, stressed, it means "visit": *jag ska hälsa **på** min mormor* (I'm going to visit my grandma). Without the particle, it means "greet": *hälsa till din familj!* (say hello to your family!). Think of English *call* vs *call on*: one small word changes the meaning — and in Swedish the stress on *på* makes the difference perfectly clear to a Swedish ear.

blocks.title: On the phone in Swedish
items: **Hej, det är Dian.** — Hi, it's Dian. (not *jag är* — on the phone it's always *det är*, just like English "it's Dian", not "I am Dian")
**Kan jag få prata med Elin?** — Could I speak to Elin?
**Ett ögonblick.** — Just a moment.
**Hon är inte hemma just nu.** — She's not home right now.
**Kan du be henne ringa mig?** — Could you ask her to call me?
**Vi hörs!** — Talk soon! (the most common way to end a call)

blocks.text: Before leaving this unit, one short table to round it off: pronouns when they are the **object**, not the subject. English does the same thing (*I → me*, *he → him*), so the idea is already familiar.

**Dem is pronounced "dom", exactly like *de*.** Because they sound identical, Swedes themselves often mix up which one is the subject and which the object in writing — the "de or dem" debate is a national spelling quarrel that never ends. A bit like English *who* vs *whom*, or *I* vs *me* in "between you and me". You may take comfort in that.

For verbs that turn back on the subject (reflexive verbs), the object form in the third person becomes **sig** (pronounced "say") — like English *himself / herself / themselves*: *han tvättar sig* (he washes himself), *hon sätter sig* (she sits down), *de klär på sig* (they get dressed). A direct cousin of *sin* — and the same test applies.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 8
items: Name the six helping verbs from Unit 8 and their meanings without looking, then make one sentence with each.
Combine them with this unit: *Han måste ringa sin mamma*, *Hon vill hälsa på sina föräldrar*, *De ska städa sina rum*.
Notice that the helping verb changes nothing about *sin* — what decides is still who the subject is.
Oskar ringer ____ mamma varje söndag. (his own mother)
Elin bor hos ____ pappa. (her own father)
Han tog ____ cykel — den står där borta. (another man's bike)
De städar ____ rum på lördagar. (their own rooms)
____ mamma bor i Norge. (Elin's mother, as the subject of the sentence)
Hon glömde ____ paraply hemma. (her own umbrella)
Kan du hjälpa ____? (me)
Jag ringer ____ ikväll. (her)
Vi träffar ____ imorgon. (them)
De ser ____ varje dag. (us)
Jag känner ____ inte. (him)
